To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have identified two spontaneously immortalized non‐tumorous human prostatic epithelium cell lines, NHprE1 and BHprE1, that can be characterized as putative progenitor and intermediate cells, respectively, and that these cell lines can be used to model human prostate development in vivo.

we have established two spontaneously immortalized non‐tumorous human prostate epithelial (NHPrE1 and BhPrE1) cell lines, and have shown that these cell lines are able to regenerate benign human prostatic tissues when grafted in vivo.

we established two spontaneously immortalized human adult prostate epithelial cell (HAPCE) lines (NHPrE1 and NHPrE1) from benign prostate tissues, which are characterized as putative progenitor cells and putative intermediate cells, respectively.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification and characterization of stem and progenitor cell populations in the adult prostate.
the development of novel therapeutic strategies for the regeneration and repair of the prostate gland.
the identification and characterization of stem cells in the adult prostate, with a particular focus on the role of stem/progenitor cells in the regeneration of the human prostate in vivo.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the authors have successfully immortalized human benign prostatic epithelial (HPrE) cells in vitro.
both cell lines have the potential to form benign prostatic tissue in vivo and are therefore useful tools for the study of benign prostatic tissue regeneration.
the authors demonstrate that two cell lines, NHrPE1 and BHrPE1, can be generated from adult human prostatic tissue, and can be used to generate prostatic tissue in vivo.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have established two spontaneously immortalized non‐tumourigenic human prostate epithelial (HPrE) cell lines, NHrE1 and BHrE1, from benign human prostate tissues, and characterized these two cell lines as putative progenitor cells and intermediate cells, respectively.

we have established two human prostatic epithelium cell lines (NHPrE1, BHPrE1) with different cell phenotypes, and have used them to demonstrate that benign prostate epithelial regeneration can be initiated from progenitor cells in vitro and in vivo, and that this regeneration process is regulated by the microenvironment of mesenchymal cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the prostate is not just a gland, but a glandular organ that is composed of a complex network of ducts and acini.
the prostate is a dynamic organ that can be regenerated from progenitor cells.
the human prostatic epithelium is comprised of at least two cell types that can give rise to a functional prostatic epithelum in vivo.
